title: Cross-layer inference audit and synthesis manual
author: Leah O'Connor
body:
Overview:
This manual defines a repeatable, cross-layer approach for auditing inference requests that hit Redwood's serving runtime and for synthesizing findings into actionable mitigations and experiments. It codifies: runtime architecture checkpoints, kernel scheduling guardrails, profiling playbooks, benchmark integration, release gating, runbook mappings, and a short known-issues catalog with triage paths.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers owning kernels and scheduler policies
- SRE and performance owners who operate production fleets
- Applied ML engineers validating model serving fidelity
- Product/QA engineers running end-to-end latency/cost regressions

Goals and scope:
- Provide a standard investigation lifecycle from signal to mitigation (Detect -> Isolate -> Reproduce -> Diagnose -> Remediate -> Verify).
- Bridge observability signals (traces, kernel telemetry, scheduler events, KV cache hits) with actionable kernel-level and orchestration-level fixes.
- Ensure benchmark artifacts and canary results map back to concrete rollout decisions.
- Cover multi-tenant and dedicated pools; on-prem private deployments may adapt the steps but keep the contract.

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Runtime kernel scheduler: ownership: runtime-kernel-team; primary oncall: @runtime-kernel-oncall; escalation: @eng-sre
- Observability and tracing: ownership: observability-team; contact: Marco Chen
- Benchmarking and gold corpus: ownership: benchmark-ops; contact: Asha Patel
- Quality + model fidelity: ownership: applied-ml; contact: Diego Rivera

Key concepts and definitions:
- Execution fan-out: number of kernels / shards invoked to satisfy a single request token. High fan-out correlates with increased tail latency and NVLink pressure.
- Kernel isolation level: the degree to which a kernel's resources and tensors are logically partitioned (full, fractional, soft-isolated).
- Fidelity tiers: {high: exact floating-point kernels; balanced: mixed quantized kernels; low-cost: quantized/approx kernels}.
- Prefix/KV caching policy: TTL and eviction semantics for cached KV entries.

Observability contract (telemetry fields every request must include):
- request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, sequence_length, prompt_prefix_hash, kernel_map_version, kernel_id_sequence, kvcache_hit_rate (percent), batch_size, scheduling_priority, pci_e_latency_ms, queue_time_ms, execution_ns, end_to_end_latency_ms, token_count
- SLOs to monitor:
  - p50 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 120ms for interactive class;
  - p95 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 250ms;
  - p99 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 800ms;
  - kernel_error_rate: < 0.2%
  - kvcache_hit_rate (global): target >= 72% for production workloads

Profiling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Detect: automated alert triggers or benchmark drift reports list anomalies. Primary signals: sudden p99 latency jump, step-change in kernel execution_ns, increased queue_time_ms, or drop in kvcache_hit_rate.
2) Capture: spin a time-bound capture (recommended 5–10 minutes) using the live trace sampler:
   - CLI: `rwictl trace capture --req-filter 'tenant=TENANT_ID & model=MODEL' --duration 600s --sampler=adaptive`
   - Ensure kernel-level hooks are enabled (kernel-map + per-kernel counters).
3) Classify: use the classification checklist to map the dominant contributor:
   - Queueing backlog (queue_time_ms dominates) -> scheduler or admission controller misconfiguration
   - Kernel slowdown (execution_ns spike across kernel_id_sequence) -> kernel regression, thermal throttling, or memory contention
   - Fan-out change (kernel_id_sequence length increased) -> topology or model sharding change
   - KV cache drop -> cache eviction regression or prefix-hash skew
4) Reproduce: use the local sandbox replay:
   - `rwictl replay --trace <trace_id> --sandbox-profile small-gpu --max-requests 200`
   - If the repro is noisy, pin the kernel-map version and disable prefetchers to isolate the kernel path.
5) Diagnose: combine kernel latency flamegraphs (per-operator) with NVLink / PCIe counters and occupancy metrics. Typical checks: GPU occupancy sudden drop, memcpy stalls, or long kernel launches due to scheduler preemption.
6) Mitigate:
   - Short-term: adjust admission control thresholds (reduce concurrency for affected pool), enact per-tenant priority throttling, or shift traffic to compatible model variant.
   - Medium-term: rollback kernel change, tune kernel launch parameters, increase KV cache TTL for the affected prefixes.
   - Long-term: implement scheduler rewrite (see Scheduler Guardrails) or rework model shard topology.
7) Verify: re-run bench harness with the same corpus and target SLOs (see Benchmarks integration).

Scheduler guardrails (recommended safety checks for any policy change):
- Any new admission rule must declare maximum concurrency (slots), preemption_weight (0–100), and safe_fallback_variant.
- Rollout checklist for scheduler policy change (minimum):
  1. Unit tests for admission rule semantics
  2. Canary: 1% traffic with shadow tracing for 1 hour
  3. Monitor: p99 latency, kernel_error_rate, queue_time_ms, and per-kernel execution_ns
  4. Abort if p99 increases by >15% or kernel_error_rate > 0.5%

Benchmarks suite and automation (how to integrate audit findings into bench artifacts):
- Gold corpus: store representative request traces and their expected fidelity checksums in the benchmark-ops artifact store. Each corpus item is annotated with sequence length, expected kvcache_hit boolean, and latency budget.
- Sample benchmark job YAML (text representation):
  name: inference-regression-check
  target_pool: prod-balanced
  corpus: gs://bench-artifacts/gold-corpora/2026-09/recall-5000
  concurrency_profile: [1, 4, 8, 16]
  validation:
    - latency_p95_ms: 250
    - fidelity_checksum: expected-v1.4

- Run locally: `benchctl run --job-file job.yaml --report-path ./reports/job-$(date +%F).json`
- Integrate with CI: benchmark artifacts are required for any kernel or scheduler PR that touches the runtime; failures must create a blocking defect in the PR pipeline.

Release notes and rollout gating (operational checklist):
- Every runtime release must include:
  - kernel-change summary (diff of kernel ids and a rationale)
  - scheduler policy change log (human-readable intent + machine-enforced guardrails)
  - benchmark run artifacts: canary and control groups with p50/p95/p99 and fidelity checksums
  - a short rollback playbook with command snippets and ownership

Example rollback snippets:
```
# Demote scheduler policy and drain new kernels
rwictl scheduler apply --policy-id OLD_POLICY_ID --force
rwictl node drain --selector 'kernel_map_version=new_2026_11' --timeout 600s
```

Runbooks (incident triage map):
- P99 latency spike (tier: high): follow Profiling playbook. Immediate actions: reduce admission concurrency by 30% for affected pool, enable shadow-routing to fallback variant, page runtime-kernel-team.
- Kernel OOMs (tier: critical): cordon affected nodes, mark kernel_id as quarantined, revert kernel image rollout, patch kernel memory accounting in the next patch.
- KV cache correctness regression (tier: high): disable prefix-based eviction, switch to TTL-based fallback, and run cache-consistency validation against the gold corpus.

Known issues (short catalog and mitigation pointers):
- Issue: intermittent NVLink retransmits increase memcpy stalls (ticket: RT-2026-344). Mitigation: adaptively throttle cross-GPU fan-out and schedule co-located shards where possible.
- Issue: quantized-kernel launch path increased p50 by ~12% on T4-like hardware (ticket: RT-2026-410). Mitigation: maintain a hardware compatibility matrix and pin balanced variant for T4 pools until kernel patch 2026.11.05.
- Issue: scheduler preemption pulses cause short-lived lat spikes when preemption_weight > 60. Mitigation: lower preemption_weight to 40 and increase soft-reserve slots.

Appendix A — Config reference (text table):
- admission_rule max_concurrency: integer (1..1024) — cap on concurrent requests per-slot
- admission_rule preemption_weight: integer (0..100) — higher favors higher-priority preemption
- kernel_map_version: string (semantic tag) — must be included in release notes
- kvcache_ttl_seconds: integer — default 300; increase for conversational workloads

Appendix B — Quick commands and debug snippets:
- Live small trace capture (5m): `rwictl trace capture --duration 300s --filter 'model:gemma-v2 & tenant:benchmark' --sampler=adaptive`
- Replay trace in sandbox with pinned kernel map: `rwictl replay --trace <id> --sandbox small-gpu --kernel-map 2026-11-05`
- Generate benchmark report: `benchctl report --input ./reports --format html --output ./reports/summary.html`

Appendix C — Change log and who to notify:
- 2026-02-13: initial draft — Leah O'Connor
- 2026-06-21: added scheduler guardrails and benchmark YAML examples — Marco Chen
- 2026-11-08: expanded known-issues and added rollback CLI snippets — Asha Patel

References and related pages:
- See the runtime decision graph for execution pathways, per-kernel telemetry contract, and the benchmark gold-corpus directory for canonical traces.

Notes and next steps:
- Short-term: adopt the observability contract across all capture agents (target Q1 2027).
- Medium-term: add a machine-readable policy schema and an automated canary gating job that fails PRs if p99 worsens by > 10%.
- Long-term: integrate kernel-safety proofs into CI for critical kernel changes.

If you have questions or need help applying this manual to a live incident, page the runtime-kernel-team and attach trace IDs and benchmark report links.
